newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico gives in to hunger strikers, protest ends.
newsitem.headline: Mexico gives in to hunger strikers, protest ends.

text.p: An almost fanatical hunger strike that has stirred polemic throughout Mexico ended on Wednesday after officials offered protesting street sweepers their jobs back or redundancy payments.
Supporters of the hunger strikers, some who survived for more than three months on just water and glucose, broke into euphoric cheering late Wednesday when their leaders told news of the deal.
Even the four badly weakened hold-out hunger strikers rose from their beds to join in the celebrations, witnesses said.

The deal was struck at the Interior Ministry with government officials from the southeastern state of Tabasco, who in 1995 fired the 300 street sweepers, leading to 1-1/2 years of protests, violence and life-or-death struggle that became a major embarrasment to the government of President Ernesto Zedillo.

"We had to create new posts so that we could invite 190 of them back to work, and the other 110 will be given redundancy payments so that they can dedicate themselves to private activities," Tabasco state Interior Secretary Victor Manuel Barcelo told TV Azteva television network.

At their makeshift camp on a heavily polluted highway outside the National Human Rights Commission in Mexico City, elated protest leaders declared the hunger strike over for the four remaining stalwarts who were on their 58th day of fasting.

Just three days before, hundreds of riot police with clubs had launched a bloody pre-dawn assault on the camp, forcibly carting three other hunger strikers to a hospital, including two unconscious men who were on the 97th day of self-imposed starvation.

Though Mexicans had widely feared for the lives of those two, there was broad condemnation of the crackdown. Even the National Human Rights Commission, often seen as reluctant to tackle the government, admitted that it was mishandled.
The hunger strike had quickly resumed after the police assault, without the three hospitalized protestors.

Zedillo said the police action was a humanitarian move aimed at saving lives, but that defence failed to wash with many commentators who saw it as an impatient gesture aimed at bypassing serious negotiation.
Wednesday's accord was almost bound to soothe tensions. In addition to meeting the protesters demands, the state government also dropped scores of outstanding arrest warrants against them.
